newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks resume rise, bonds rally after holiday.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks resume rise, bonds rally after holiday.

text.p: Stocks resumed their rally in a shortened session Friday as long-term interest rates fell and the holiday shopping season got off to a strong start.
The dollar rallied against major currencies and lumber prices rose.
After two sessions of losses, the Dow Jones industrial average rallied 22.36 points to close at 6,521.70, up 49.94 on the week.
In the broader market, gaining issues outpaced losers, 1,305 to 906, on very light volume of 149.8 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange as many traders stayed home for a long weekend.
Trading on the NYSE, Nasdaq and the American Stock Exchange closed at 1 p.m. EST in a shortened, post-holiday session. Financial markets were closed for the Thanksgiving holiday on Thursday.
The Nasdaq composite index, laden with technology stocks, rose 5.29 to a 1,292.61, a fifth consecutive record. It was up 18.25 for the week.

"The market still has an upward bias, so unless we get some bad news, it's going to keep going up. Also, it's apparently going to be a good Christmas for retailers," said Jim Benning, a trader at BT Brokerage.

Despite a shorter post-Thanksgiving shopping season, analysts said they expect holiday sales to jump about 5 percent over last year's disappointing season due to higher consumer confidence and strong employment.

"The stock market knows no bounds," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "It's going to be a strong Christmas season for retailers, and the economy is no longer tepid."

Stocks also got a boost from the bond market, where the benchmark 30-year Treasury rose nearly a full point, knocking the yield down to 6.36 percent, the lowest since March 4, from 6.45 percent on Wednesday. Prices and yields move in the opposite direction in the bond market.
Falling long-term rates tend to drive money into stocks.
In currency markets, the dollar rose against major currencies as European leaders reiterated their desire for a stronger dollar and interest rates tumbled in Europe's bond markets.
the dollar rose to 1.5386 German marks from 1.5320 marks at Thursday's European close and to 113.84 Japanese yen from 113.62.
Elsewhere, lumber prices soared in light trading amid expectations that cash prices will soon recover from a severe two-week drop.

Cash lumber prices have fallen nearly $100 per 1,000 board feet since early November. Cash spruce, a key species used in home-building, went from $473 per 1,000 board feet on Nov. 15 to $378 on Wednesday, according to Random Lengths, a leading lumber market service.
January lumber finished up the $10 limit up at $392.20 per 1,000 board feet at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange. The March contract rose $8.20 to $378.70.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 rose 7.8 points to 4,058.0, gaining 39.3 on the week. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 average lost 15.18 points to 21,020.36, a fall of 195.75 from last Friday.
